segments.title: Introduction of the Heritage program; music is music
segments.summary: The host introduces Armstrong and guests Benny Benack and Frederick Dorian. Armstrong says a note is a note in any language.

segments.title: European musicians and jazz as an international language
segments.summary: Asked if Europeans look to America, Armstrong says musicians everywhere play the same music, and foreign arrangers wrote for the big bands.

segments.title: New Orleans funeral marches, brass bands and the first-chair trumpet
segments.summary: Asked about European composers using jazz, Armstrong describes expressing yourself in funeral marches and the Star-Spangled Banner, and why the lead trumpet matters.

segments.title: Improvising, Princess Margaret, Robert Merrill, and symphony versus jazz feeling
segments.summary: Armstrong explains how he improvises around the lead, mentions playing for Princess Margaret and singing with Robert Merrill, and says jazz is subjective while symphonic playing is objective. He recalls playing silent pictures in a 1925 Chicago theater orchestra and Cavalleria rusticana.

segments.title: Never changing his style; sincerity and a Pittsburgh jam session
segments.summary: Armstrong says he never changed his way of playing and that sincerity matters. He criticizes youngsters showing off, citing a Pittsburgh jam session with nine saxophones.

segments.title: Jamming versus recording and late nights with Bix Beiderbecke
segments.summary: Armstrong says jamming and record dates are played the same way, though jam tapes get commercialized. He recalls Bix at the Sunset in Chicago after hours, and says he enjoys everything he plays.

segments.title: Advice to young players: learn everything
segments.summary: Asked how young people should become jazz musicians, Armstrong says to be a good musician who can play symphony or blues.

segments.title: Staying fit to play trumpet and the warm-up routine
segments.summary: Armstrong talks about quitting at 35, caring for stomach and lips, physical condition, and his warm-up. The talk turns to Dixieland, with a commercial break.

segments.chapter: Classical roots and the future of jazz
segments.title: Jazz with symphony orchestras and playing silent pictures
segments.summary: Armstrong says his band sat in with Bernstein's orchestra and says jazz and symphony should play together. He tells a story about accompanying an Indian-tribe scene in a silent film.

segments.chapter: Classical roots and the future of jazz
segments.title: Classical composers, orphanage music and the staying power of jazz
segments.summary: Armstrong lists the classical composers he played in the orphanage and brass bands, discusses foreign arrangers and symphonic hot-man work, and dismisses fads like bop and rock and roll.

segments.chapter: Classical roots and the future of jazz
segments.title: Program sign-off
segments.summary: The host closes the program and credits WQED Pittsburgh and National Educational Television.
